svg.title: P031. Why does only Asha qualify?
svg.desc: The exact saved SQLite query starts with Orders and joins customer names. The customer totals are 300, 100, and 200. Their average is 200. Only Asha Rao passes the strict greater-than test and is 50 percent above average.
svg.text: Follow the locked query from the order rows to one customer above the average.
Which rows do we start with?
FROM Orders AS o supplies every purchase amount, including orders without a matching customer.
Order 10 carries customer ID 1 and an amount of 300. The name for ID 1 is Asha Rao.
How does each order get its customer name?
Orders supplies CustomerID. LEFT JOIN adds the name before grouping and keeps unmatched orders.
LEFT JOIN Customers AS c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
3 order rows → 3 joined rows. For order 10, o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID = 1.
If ID 99 had no customer record, its order would keep its amount and the query would label it ‘Unknown’.
What is one customer’s total spend?
Group by o.CustomerID, c.FirstName and c.LastName. SUM adds the amounts inside each group.
customer_spend has 3 customer rows. Each customer has one order in this practice example.
If Asha’s 300 were split into orders of 100 and 200, her group would still produce one total of 300.
Why does the same average appear three times?
The scalar subquery reads the totals in customer_spend. It returns one value for all three rows.
spend_with_avg still has 3 rows. Each customer contributes exactly once to the average.
The outer query starts with spend_with_avg. WHERE tests each total against the unrounded average.
3 customer rows → 1 qualifying row. Cia is exactly at 200, so the strict > excludes her.
How far above average is Asha?
Subtract the average, divide by that same average, then express the difference as a percentage.
NULLIF guards against a zero denominator. ORDER BY total_spend DESC puts the highest spend first.
